title: The daily mental routine
teaches: Run the trading day in three parts: a warm-up before the open (game plan, levels, your own state, if-then rules), breaks and check-ins during the session, and a written cool-down after the close that picks one thing to improve tomorrow.

facts.quote: Notice how in most performance activities, top performers engage in warm up exercises. Singers, musicians, athletes--all have their warm up routines.
facts.claim: In most performance fields, top performers warm up before they perform.

facts.quote: Your trading warm up should put you in the mental, physical, and emotional state you need to be in to do your best trading.
facts.claim: A trading warm-up readies your mind, body and emotions, not just your charts.

facts.quote: Many, many trading problems occur simply because the right functions were never warmed up.
facts.claim: Many trading problems start because the trader never warmed up.

facts.quote: I love to mentally rehearse different market scenarios as we approach the open. The scenarios include how I would respond to early weakness or strength
facts.claim: Before the open, Steenbarger rehearses how he would respond to early weakness or strength.

facts.quote: Warm ups practice the functions we most want to employ.
facts.claim: A warm-up practises the skills you are about to use.

facts.quote: Contemplating many market possibilities helps ensure I don't get locked into any one.
facts.claim: Rehearsing several scenarios keeps you from getting locked into one view.

facts.quote: Review before trading starts to ensure that the rules are being followed in generating ideas, with special emphasis on the rules relevant to the prior day's trading;
facts.claim: Steenbarger reviews his written rules before trading starts.

facts.quote: Review at the end of trading to assess whether rules were followed and especially to look at how a following of the rules could have improved the day's trading;
facts.claim: At the end of the trading day he checks whether he followed his rules.

facts.quote: Targeting one or more rules to focus on for the coming session to improve trading.
facts.claim: He then picks a rule or two to focus on in the next session.

facts.quote: What if, at any given time, we worked on one goal and one goal only. Suppose we worked on it every single day and made it the focus on each day's efforts.
facts.claim: Steenbarger suggests working on one goal at a time, every day.

facts.quote: By setting a large number of goals, traders have difficulties prioritizing the changes they want to make, and they find it difficult to give each of the goals proper attention.
facts.claim: With too many goals, none of them gets proper attention.

facts.quote: A vague goal is only a good intention; it's not likely to energize or shape performance. My experience is that vague goals get the least follow-through.
facts.claim: Vague goals get the least follow-through.

facts.quote: Elite performers--in music, theater, professional sports, chess--spend more time practicing and preparing than actually performing in competition.
facts.claim: Elite performers spend more time practising and preparing than performing.

facts.quote: Trading without review is like playing a football game without huddles; like preparing for a baseball or basketball game without practices or review of game film.
facts.claim: Trading without review is like playing sport without practice or game film.

facts.quote: Ideas must include entries/stops/targets/risk amount
facts.claim: In an SMB trader's morning routine that Steenbarger published, every idea needs an entry, stop, target and risk amount.

facts.quote: If you're not working on change daily, you're not working on change. And if you try to accomplish massive changes in one day, you run the risk of activating competing motivations and derailing your efforts.
facts.claim: Change is a daily job, and trying to change everything at once tends to derail it.

facts.quote: But most of us are far from ideal and need to change one action at a time.
facts.claim: Steenbarger passes on a point he calls excellent: most of us need to change one action at a time.

facts.quote: The key to remaking yourself is to find the small steps that add to big changes without setting off alarms.
facts.claim: Small steps add up to big changes.

facts.quote: I find that a surprising proportion of what sets traders up for success during the day is what has happened the previous night.
facts.claim: Much of what sets up a good trading day happens the night before.

facts.quote: One study found that financial decision making was meaningfully impaired when subjects were sleepy due to poorer judgment about the task being undertaken.
facts.claim: Steenbarger cites a study in which sleepy people made worse financial decisions.

facts.quote: If we make decisions in cognitive, emotional, and physical states that are different from the ones we occupied during our preparation, we're likely to find that the decisions we plan won't always be the ones we act upon.
facts.claim: A plan made in one state won't always be the one you act on in a different state.

facts.quote: Preparation puts emotion into perspective; we gain control, not by staying Zen, but by anticipating situations that are likely to take us out of calm focus and preparing our responses to those.
facts.claim: You gain control by planning your response to the situations that throw you off.

facts.quote: We cannot--and should not--eliminate emotion from trading, but that is also not necessary.
facts.claim: The goal is not to have no emotion while trading.

facts.quote: At the end of the day, week, and month, you can track what you did well and what needs improvement.
facts.claim: Review at the end of each day, week and month: what went well and what needs work.

facts.quote: Both provide opportunities for goal setting, as you have goals to repeat and expand what you did well and goals to correct what you didn't do well.
facts.claim: What you did well becomes a goal to repeat; what you did badly becomes a goal to correct.

facts.quote: Note how in every performance activity--acting, music, sports, dancing--there are active practice sessions that accomplish two purposes: they keep the performer in shape, and they rehearse the challenges that are likely to be faced during live performance.
facts.claim: Every performance field has practice sessions that keep the performer in shape and rehearse live challenges.

facts.quote: The routines of trading are what enable us to process market information efficiently and stick to what we do best.
facts.claim: Routines let you process the market efficiently and stick to what you do best.

facts.quote: If you identify a best practice in your trading, the best thing you can do is transform it into a robust habit pattern. A definition of good trading could be: doing automatically what you would ideally do by choice.
facts.claim: Turn your best practices into habits, so you do the right thing automatically.

facts.quote: Routine is the friend of efficiency and the enemy of change.
facts.claim: Routines make you efficient but can stop you from changing.

facts.quote: There is a world of difference between the person with five years of experience and the person who repeats a year's experience five times.
facts.claim: Repeating the same year is not the same as growing for five years.

facts.quote: It's the reworking of old trading processes and the addition of new ones that enable traders to stay profitable when markets go from trending and non-volatile to volatile and choppy.
facts.claim: Reworking your processes is what keeps you profitable when markets turn choppy.

facts.quote: We act as if experience itself will teach us all we need to know, when it is guided experience--experience informed by goals and feedback--that gets us where we want to go.
facts.claim: Experience teaches best when it is guided by goals and feedback.

facts.quote: My trading day begins early in the morning with an assessment of overseas markets, an advance look at economic reports due for the day, a review of the prior day's market indicators
facts.claim: Steenbarger's trading day starts with overseas markets, the day's scheduled economic reports and yesterday's indicators.

facts.quote: We become fatigued, and in the fatigued state we're more likely to make mistakes and fall into old habit patterns that cost us money.
facts.claim: When you're fatigued, mistakes and old bad habits become more likely.

facts.quote: Either you battle test your plans in rehearsal mode or they will be tested in actual battle.
facts.claim: Rehearse your plan before the session, or the market will test it for you.

facts.quote: When we establish a routine--and then make it routine--we take our strengths and make them automatic.
facts.claim: A routine you keep turns your strengths into automatic habits.

facts.quote: If you are focused on small wins and the processes that generate profits over time, however, the coming week can always be a successful one.
facts.claim: Judge yourself on the process that makes money over time, not on one day's result.

facts.quote: When we study our successes and figure out how we are making use of our strengths at those times, we become able to define our best practices.
facts.claim: Studying your successes is how you find your best practices.

facts.quote: When it comes to your Mental Game, I typically focus on four major areas for winning routines: Daily Overall Routine Pre-Session Warm Up In-Session/Tournament Routine Post-Session Cool Down
facts.claim: Tendler's routine has four parts: the daily basics, a warm-up before, a routine during, and a cool-down after the session.

facts.quote: If your routines need improvement, start small. Look for just one thing you can add that can make a slight improvement.
facts.claim: Improve a routine one small addition at a time.

facts.quote: Your daily routine covers the basics: what and when you eat, exercise, recharge, and sleep.
facts.claim: The daily routine covers food, exercise, recharging and sleep.

facts.quote: Before you begin trading or playing poker, you need to get your mind ready – much like an athlete readies their body to compete.
facts.claim: Get your mind ready before you trade, the way an athlete readies the body.

facts.quote: Without this, you won't be sharp when you start and are at risk of mistakes or missing opportunities.
facts.claim: Skip the warm-up and you start dull, at risk of mistakes and missed chances.

facts.quote: For traders, that sometimes means reviewing overnight sessions, looking at stock screeners or TA levels, and gauging what symbols you are looking for that day.
facts.claim: The strategic part of the warm-up: overnight action, screens, levels and today's names.

facts.quote: Both traders and poker players should also include a mental game plan to address the problems that are most likely to affect you – such as tilt, boredom, focus
facts.claim: The warm-up includes a plan for the mental problems most likely to hit you.

facts.quote: My best advice here is to not wait until you need it. Find your trend, or key on early warning signs, so you can take a break before your energy nosedives.
facts.claim: Take a break before your energy drops, not after.

facts.quote: But fatigue decreases your ability to control your emotions and emotional volatility increases your chances of making a mistake.
facts.claim: Fatigue weakens emotional control, and that raises the odds of a mistake.

facts.quote: What you do after the session or event is all about tomorrow.
facts.claim: The cool-down is preparation for tomorrow.

facts.quote: Sometimes we rely too much on our memory. As soon as you walk away, details start to disappear.
facts.claim: Details fade as soon as you walk away, so write them down.

facts.quote: On days where there was some significant emotion, the goal is to reduce the chance of that emotion carrying over to the following day.
facts.claim: After an emotional day, the cool-down aims to stop the emotion carrying into tomorrow.

facts.quote: At a minimum, do a brain dump, writing out everything in your mind, what happened, what the emotion was, what the trigger was
facts.claim: At minimum, write out what happened, what you felt and what triggered it.

facts.quote: While they don't guarantee that you will perform at your best, they do make it more likely.
facts.claim: Routines don't guarantee your best performance; they make it more likely.

facts.quote: Obviously there are no guarantees that winning routines will translate into winning results, but they definitely increase the probability
facts.claim: Good routines raise the odds of good results, with no guarantee.

facts.quote: If you don't, the chance you will make the same mistake again goes up and nothing is more frustrating than making the same mistake over and over.
facts.claim: Skip the cool-down and you are more likely to repeat the same mistake.

facts.quote: What did you do well in general and/or improve on the things you've been working on? What mistakes did you make? How can you improve on them and/or be better next time?
facts.claim: Tendler's three cool-down questions: what went well, what mistakes you made, how to improve next time.

facts.quote: You need to get the emotion out and the best time to do it is soon after you're done.
facts.claim: The best time to process a session's emotion is soon after it ends.

facts.quote: To create your bubble, write for up to 15 minutes, one hour before you start to play/trade.
facts.claim: Before trading, write out what's on your mind for up to 15 minutes.

facts.quote: This gives you an opportunity to get some of the emotion out and/or make a list of tasks, with the intent of being able to put them away for now.
facts.claim: Writing it out lets you put outside worries away for the session.

facts.quote: you go through waves where you do it regularly, only to fall off during periods when you're doing quite well, evidence of some subtle overconfidence weakening your process.
facts.claim: Dropping the journal when things go well is a sign of subtle overconfidence.

facts.quote: the idea is to eventually reach the point where it's so ingrained as part of your daily routine that you can't not do it.
facts.claim: The aim is a habit so ingrained you do it without forcing it.

facts.quote: when you're tired, or burnt out, your emotions get bigger while your ability to deal with them is more limited.
facts.claim: Tired, your emotions grow and your ability to handle them shrinks.

facts.quote: Traders should at least have written "if, then" plans to help limit emotion-based actions and prevent additional big losses and should consciously commit to these plans before every trading session.
facts.claim: Write if-then plans and commit to them before every session.

facts.quote: For example, they could pledge to step away for the day if they lose a certain amount of money or take 15 minutes if they feel an urge to break a trading rule.
facts.claim: Examples: stop for the day after a set loss, or take 15 minutes when you feel the urge to break a rule.

facts.quote: Writing about worries before a high-pressure event frees up working memory, allowing more capacity to focus on the task at hand.
facts.claim: Writing out worries before a high-pressure event frees attention for the task.

facts.quote: If a trader mentally practices the ideal response to certain situations, it should help them execute when those situations arise for real.
facts.claim: Mentally practising your response helps you carry it out for real.

facts.quote: Studies have consistently linked intense emotional reactions to poor trading performance.
facts.claim: Intense emotional reactions go with poor trading performance.

facts.quote: Psychological studies suggest that when athletes write about performance failures, it can reduce the mental impact and help them reframe the event as a set of lessons instead.
facts.claim: Writing about a failure can soften its impact and turn it into lessons.

facts.quote: Whatever the reason for the blowup, traders can get past it, but positive thinking alone won't do the trick.
facts.claim: Positive thinking alone does not fix a trading problem.

facts.quote: If a trader has trouble distancing their emotions from their trading decisions, it's never a bad idea to slow down or even take a break. Cooler heads usually prevail, and trading is no exception.
facts.claim: When emotion creeps into decisions, slow down or take a break.

facts.quote: Even seasoned traders can find buying and selling near the opening and closing bells a bit like surfing when waves are biggest—if they misread the conditions, they might get hurt.
facts.claim: Trading near the open is hard even for experienced traders.

facts.quote: But when news breaks outside of trading hours, an imbalance between buy and sell orders may cause a stock to open dramatically higher or lower than its price at the previous close.
facts.claim: News outside trading hours can make a stock open far from its prior close.

facts.quote: Trading in the market is about probabilities, not certainties.
facts.claim: Trading is about probabilities, not certainties.

facts.quote: Don't play it by ear—you must have some pre-fixed levels in your mind for every stock you plan to trade.

facts.quote: But as a novice, it is better to just read the market without making any moves for the first 15–20 minutes.

facts.quote: knowing the latest in the stock markets, keeping track of events that affect stocks
facts.claim: Keep track of the events that move stocks.

facts.claim: Revise your plan regularly: add what works, drop what doesn't.

facts.quote: Don't try to make up for a losing trade by trading more. Revenge trading is a recipe for disaster.
facts.claim: Don't trade more to win back a loss.

facts.claim: Stay away from stock boards and chat rooms.

facts.quote: Discipline can't be taught in a seminar or found in expensive trading software.
facts.claim: Discipline doesn't come from software or seminars.

facts.quote: The only way to achieve long-term success is with hard work and discipline.
facts.claim: Long-term success comes from hard work and discipline.

facts.quote: We find that subjects whose emotional reaction to monetary gains and losses was more intense on both the positive and negative side exhibited significantly worse trading performance.

facts.quote: We investigate several possible links between psychological factors and trading performance in a sample of 80 anonymous day-traders.
facts.claim: The study followed 80 day traders.

facts.quote: If trading is indeed a performance field, there is no reason to believe that elite performance will be found in better indicators, faster or more comprehensive software, newsletter tips, or coaching advice.
facts.claim: If trading is a performance field, elite performance won't come from better tools or tips.

facts.quote: Only a directed developmental process will allow you to internalize market patterns and act upon these with confidence.
facts.claim: Only directed development lets you learn market patterns and act on them with confidence.

facts.quote: In sum, my best advice is to truly treat trading as a profession if it is to be your career.
facts.claim: Steenbarger and Toghraie's advice: treat trading as a profession.

facts.quote: Better golf clubs will not turn a duffer into a pro; the finest wrenches will not make one a master mechanic.
facts.claim: Better tools don't make a professional.

facts.quote: Core Trading Session: 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET
facts.claim: The NYSE core session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Take your time and don't ever invest in anything you haven't thoroughly and independently researched.
facts.claim: Never buy anything you haven't researched yourself.

facts.claim: Our rule: never trade an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size.

walkthroughs.title: Trading is a performance
steps: Singers, musicians, athletes. Nobody serious walks out cold. They warm up first, and so should you.
Treat trading like a profession. The best performers spend more time preparing than performing.
So your day has three parts. Warm up, trade, cool down.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open
steps: Start with the game plan. Today's names, the levels, and an entry, stop and size for each one.
Then check the trader. How you slept, what's on your mind, which mistake is most likely to bite today.
Write an if-then for that mistake, like a 15-minute break when the urge hits. Commit to it before the bell.
Tired, sick, angry or distracted, and it's a no-new-trades day. That's part of the plan too.

walkthroughs.title: During and after
steps: During the session, trade the plan. Take a short break before you're drained, not after.
After the close, write it up while it's fresh. What went well, what went wrong, what you'd do better.
Then pick one thing to work on tomorrow. One thing, and specific. Small steps every day add up.

questions.q: Singers, musicians and pro athletes all do one thing before they perform. What should you copy from them before the open?
choices: Run a warm-up routine first
Start cold and ease into it
Do a lucky ritual
Rest up to save your energy
questions.why: Warm up first. Nobody serious walks on stage cold, and the open is our stage. A warm-up practises the exact skills you're about to use: reading the chart, sticking to your levels, taking your stop. Skip it and your first few trades become the warm-up. That's where the sloppy entries and the missed setups come from. I want to be sharp on the first trade, not the fifth.
questions.lesson_line: Nobody good performs cold. Warm up before the open.

wrong.Start cold and ease into it: Then your first trades are the warm-up, and you pay for them. Cold is when you miss the trigger or fumble the order.
wrong.Do a lucky ritual: A ritual for luck has no job to do. A warm-up has one: it practises what you're about to do.
wrong.Rest up to save your energy: Rest is for the night before. The time before the open is for getting your head in the game.

questions.simple: Warm up first, because a warm-up gets your head sharp before the first trade, not after it.

reasons: two publishers agree (Steenbarger, Tendler); a stable idea

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger, a trading coach, points out that singers, musicians and athletes all have warm-up routines, and that warm-ups practise the functions we most want to use. Jared Tendler: before you trade, get your mind ready, much like an athlete readies their body. Without it you won't be sharp when you start.

questions.q: You want a daily routine you can run every single session. How do you lay out the trading day?
choices: Warm up, trade, cool down
Trade first, warm up as you go
Warm up, trade, then log off
Plan Sunday, then trade all week
questions.why: Three parts: warm up, trade, cool down. Every day. The warm-up gets your levels and your head ready before the bell. During the session you trade the plan and take breaks. After the close you write it up and pick what to fix tomorrow. That last part is the one most people skip, and it's the one that makes you better. A Sunday review is great, but it rides on top of the daily one. It doesn't replace it.
questions.lesson_line: Before the open, during the session, after the close. Every day.

wrong.Trade first, warm up as you go: Then the market's your warm-up, and it charges for it. Get ready before your first order.
wrong.Warm up, trade, then log off: That skips the review. What you do after the close is all about tomorrow.
wrong.Plan Sunday, then trade all week: A weekly plan helps, but the routine is daily. Every session gets its own warm-up and its own write-up.

questions.simple: Warm up, trade, cool down, because you get ready before the bell and learn from the day after it.

reasons: two publishers agree (Tendler, Steenbarger); a stable idea

deeper.example: Jared Tendler builds routines around a warm-up before the session, a routine during it and a cool-down after it. Brett Steenbarger reviews his rules before trading starts and again at the end of trading, then targets one or more rules to focus on in the coming session.

questions.q: Checking your own mood and focus belongs in your warm-up, right next to your charts and levels.
questions.why: True. The charts are half the job. You're the other half. Before the bell I want to know what kind of head I'm in. Tired, still mad about yesterday's loss, or bored and itching to press buttons. Name the problem most likely to hit you today and decide how you'll handle it. A clean watchlist doesn't help much if the person trading it is on tilt, trading off emotion instead of the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Warm up the trader, not just the watchlist.
questions.simple: True, because a warm-up gets your head ready too, not just your charts.

reasons: two publishers agree (Steenbarger, Tendler); a stable idea

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger: your trading warm-up should put you in the mental, physical and emotional state you need to do your best trading. Jared Tendler adds a mental game plan for the problems most likely to affect you, such as tilt, boredom and focus.

questions.q: Five names on your watchlist for today. What do you write down for each one before the bell?
choices: Its entry, stop and size
What the chat room thinks
Nothing, decide at the open
Today's profit goal
questions.why: Entry, stop and size, for every name. Every buy we make has those three written down before the market opens. At the open things move fast. You don't want to be doing math with your finger on the button. Decide the trigger, the stop and the share count while you're calm, then set an alert at each trigger. Now the open is just execution. It doesn't mean you buy all five. It means nothing gets bought without a plan.
questions.lesson_line: Every name on today's list gets its levels before the bell.

wrong.What the chat room thinks: That's someone else's idea, not your plan. We never take a trade off an alert, a post or a video without our own entry, stop and size.
wrong.Nothing, decide at the open: That's playing it by ear at the fastest, noisiest part of the day. Set your levels before the bell.
wrong.Today's profit goal: A dollar goal is a result you don't control. Plan what you do control: where you get in, where you're wrong, how big.

questions.simple: Write each name's entry, stop and size before the bell, so the open is execution, not guesswork.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, F66)
fixed before (chat-room note)

deeper.example: An SMB trader's morning plan, published by Brett Steenbarger, needs entries, stops, targets and a risk amount for every idea. Investopedia: don't play it by ear, have pre-fixed levels in mind for every stock you plan to trade.

questions.q: Your trading day really starts the night before, with how well you sleep.
questions.why: True. A bad night shows up in your trading the next day. One study found sleepy people made worse money decisions. So tonight is part of tomorrow's prep. The basics matter: when you eat, when you exercise, when you shut it down and sleep. There's no magic number of hours here. Just check it in your warm-up. If you slept badly and feel tired, that's a no-new-trades day for us.
questions.lesson_line: Tomorrow's warm-up starts with tonight's sleep.
questions.simple: True, because how you slept shows up in how you trade the next day.

reasons: two publishers agree (Steenbarger, Tendler); no number taught

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger finds that a surprising proportion of what sets traders up for success during the day is what happened the previous night. He cites a study where sleepy subjects made worse financial decisions. Jared Tendler's daily routine covers what and when you eat, exercise, recharge and sleep.

questions.q: You want to get a lot better at trading this year. Where does that improvement really come from?
choices: Practice, prep and review
Sharper chart indicators
Hot tips from other traders
Natural talent and instinct
questions.why: Practice, prep and review. Look at the fields where people perform under pressure, like sport, music and chess. The best spend more time practising and preparing than performing. Trading's the same. A new indicator is still you reading it, and a tip is someone else's read. The reps are what build you: prep before the open, trade the plan, review the film after. Nobody sells discipline. You build it.
questions.lesson_line: Train like an athlete: prep, perform, review. Better tools don't replace the reps.

wrong.Natural talent and instinct: Talent helps, but top performers in sport, music and chess still practise more than they perform. The work comes first.
wrong.Sharper chart indicators: Better golf clubs don't turn a hacker into a pro. Same with indicators. The skill is in you, not the screen.
wrong.Hot tips from other traders: A tip is someone else's read. Use it as an idea if you like, then do your own work: your entry, your stop, your size.

questions.simple: Practice, prep and review, because top performers in sport and music practise more than they perform.

reasons: the newsletter-tips line is an open owner note in conflicts (UCT runs alerts and a newsletter)
fixed before

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger: elite performers in music, theater, sports and chess spend more time practicing and preparing than performing. In a Fidelity piece he co-wrote with Adrienne Toghraie: elite performance won't be found in better indicators, faster software or newsletter tips, and better golf clubs will not turn a duffer into a pro. Investopedia: discipline can't be found in expensive trading software.

questions.q: Finish the line. It sums up Tendler's advice on improving a routine.
questions.sentence: When your routine needs work, add new things ___ at a time.
questions.why: One. Tendler: when your routines need work, start small and look for just one thing you can add. Steenbarger says change is a daily job. Try massive changes in one day and you risk derailing your efforts. This does not mean your routine stays small. Small steps add up to big changes.
questions.lesson_line: One small change you keep beats a big overhaul you drop.
questions.simple: One, because a single small change you can keep beats trying to fix everything at once.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: You've run the same routine every day for months. What's it supposed to turn your trading into?
choices: The right moves become automatic
Never feeling any fear or greed
Taking every setup that shows up
Winning more trades than you lose
questions.why: The right moves become automatic. That's the whole point of a routine. Find what you do well, then repeat it until you can't not do it. Writing the plan, setting the stop, taking the loss when it's hit. When those run on autopilot, you stop burning energy fighting yourself. It doesn't mean you stop feeling things. You'll still feel fear and greed. The habits just carry you through it.
questions.lesson_line: Repeat the right steps until you don't need the checklist.

wrong.Winning more trades than you lose: That's an outcome, and you don't control it. Good trading is about what you do, trade after trade.
wrong.Never feeling any fear or greed: Not happening, and you don't need it. You can't remove emotion from trading. The routine works with it.
wrong.Taking every setup that shows up: That's overtrading. A routine keeps you on what you do best, not on everything that moves.

questions.simple: The right moves become automatic, because a routine you keep turns your best habits into things you don't have to force.

reasons: fixed before (key reworded to keep 'ideally')

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger: a definition of good trading could be doing automatically what you would ideally do by choice. When we establish a routine and make it routine, we take our strengths and make them automatic. Jared Tendler wants a habit so ingrained that you can't not do it.

questions.q: Your levels are set for today's names. What else needs checking before the bell?
choices: Earnings dates and overnight news
Nothing, the charts are enough
Where the market will close
A plan to win back yesterday's loss
questions.why: Earnings dates and overnight news. Check the date on every name. We don't buy in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report can gap a stock right past your stop overnight, and no stop can catch that. Then scan the overnight news. News outside market hours can open a stock far above or below where it closed, and your levels need to know that. Fed and CPI days are different. Know they're coming, but we trade them like any other day.
questions.lesson_line: Before the bell, know every name's earnings date and the overnight news.

wrong.Where the market will close: Nobody knows that. Trading's about probabilities, not certainties. Prep what's on the calendar, not a forecast.
wrong.Nothing, the charts are enough: Charts don't show tonight's news or next week's report. A gap open can blow right through your levels.
wrong.A plan to win back yesterday's loss: That's revenge trading, planned ahead of time. Trading more to make up a loss is a recipe for disaster.

questions.simple: Check earnings dates and overnight news, because a report or a news gap can blow right past your levels.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, C32)

questions.story: You know your weak spot. After a losing trade, you rush right into the next one. Today's charts and levels are done.
questions.q: What else goes in your warm-up today?
choices: A written if-then plan for it
Nothing, the charts are all set
A note to stay positive
Smaller size on every trade
questions.answer: A written if-then plan for it
questions.why: Write an if-then plan for it. You already know how this one goes, so decide the answer now, while you're calm. Something like: if I take a loss and feel the itch to jump back in, then I stand up and take 15 minutes. If the setup triggers again, it's a new trade with its own stop. Write it down before the bell. In the moment, the sting of the loss argues louder than any good intention. A plan you made calm wins that argument.
questions.lesson_line: Know your pattern. Write the plan for it before the bell, not after the damage.

wrong.Nothing, the charts are all set: The charts are ready. You aren't. A pattern you already know needs its own plan.
wrong.A note to stay positive: Positive thinking alone won't stop the rush. You need a specific move, decided ahead of time.
wrong.Smaller size on every trade: That makes the rush cheaper, not rarer. Fix the habit. We don't cut size after losses. Only a drawdown in the account does that.

questions.simple: Write an if-then plan for it, because a response you decided calmly beats the rush you feel after a loss.

deeper.example: Written before the open: if I feel the urge to jump straight back in after a loss, then I stand up and take 15 minutes before the next order. If the setup triggers again, then it's a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Jared Tendler's warm-up includes a plan for the problems most likely to affect you. Schwab suggests written if-then plans, committed to before every session.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21); Schwab's other example, stepping away for the day after a set loss, is a daily loss limit our rule (B15) rejects, so it is not taught

questions.q: Before the open you run through it: if the market rips early I'll do this, if it dumps I'll do that. Why bother?
choices: To follow the plan when it's real
To predict where the market opens
To find more reasons to trade
To take emotion out of it
questions.answer: To follow the plan when it's real
questions.why: So you actually follow the plan when it's real. A plan made calm before the bell doesn't always survive a fast open. You're in a different head by then. Rehearsing closes that gap. You've already seen the early dump in your mind and already know what you'll do, so you just do it. Either you test the plan in rehearsal, or the market tests it with your money. And it's not a forecast. Running a few scenarios keeps you from marrying one.
questions.lesson_line: Rehearse the response before the bell, so the market isn't your first test.

wrong.To predict where the market opens: Rehearsal isn't a forecast. You run several scenarios so you don't get stuck on one.
wrong.To find more reasons to trade: Rehearsal is about how you respond, not how often you trade.
wrong.To take emotion out of it: You can't remove emotion, and you don't need to. You prepare your response so emotion doesn't make the call.

questions.simple: So you follow the plan for real, because a response you've practised is easier to carry out under pressure.

reasons: fixed before

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger mentally rehearses how he'd respond to early weakness or strength as the open approaches. His line: either you battle test your plans in rehearsal mode or they will be tested in actual battle. Schwab: if a trader mentally practices the ideal response, it should help them execute when the situation arises for real.

questions.q: Finish Tendler's three cool-down questions.
questions.sentence: What did I do well? What mistakes did I make? How can I ___ next time?
questions.why: Improve. Tendler asks three questions after a session: what you did well, what mistakes you made, and how to improve next time. Steenbarger's review tracks what you did well and what needs improvement, at the end of each day, week and month. The cool-down is about tomorrow, not today's score.
questions.lesson_line: Three questions after every session: what worked, what didn't, what changes tomorrow.
questions.simple: Improve, because the third question turns today's mistakes into a change you make next time.

reasons: two publishers agree (Tendler, Steenbarger); a stable idea

questions.q: Getting really fired up after a big win is harmless to your trading.
questions.why: False. A big high after a win can hurt you the same way a big low after a loss can. In a study of 80 day traders, the ones who reacted more intensely to gains and to losses traded significantly worse. It's one study, and it shows a link, not proof. But think about how it plays out. You hit a big winner, you feel bulletproof, and the next trade gets sloppy. That's also why we never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners. Feeling good is fine. Feeling invincible is the warning sign.
questions.lesson_line: Check in after big wins too. A big high is a warning sign, just like a big low.
questions.simple: False, because a big high after a win can make you sloppy, just like a big low after a loss.

deeper.counter: Feeling good after a win is normal and not the problem. Steenbarger, one of the study's authors, says we cannot and should not remove emotion from trading. The warning is about intensity: a big high, like a big low, is a state to notice before the next order.

reasons: NBER study plus Schwab; the 80 is in the quote and does not change

questions.story: A fight with your landlord is still on your mind. The open is an hour away.
questions.q: What do you do with it first?
choices: Write it out, then set it aside
Push it down and focus on charts
Trade to take your mind off it
Cut your size to allow for it
questions.answer: Write it out, then set it aside
questions.why: Write it out, then put it away. Grab a notebook and write for up to 15 minutes: what happened, how you feel, what you'll do about it later. Getting it on paper frees up the part of your head the market needs. Then it waits until after the close. If it's still eating at you at the open, that's a distracted day. Distracted means no new trades for us.
questions.lesson_line: Get it on paper, then draw a line under it. It waits until after the close.

wrong.Push it down and focus on charts: Pushed down, it keeps tugging at you all morning. Writing it out clears the space.
wrong.Trade to take your mind off it: That's putting money on a distracted head. A trade isn't a way to stop thinking about something.
wrong.Cut your size to allow for it: Smaller size doesn't clear your head. Write it out first. Still distracted at the open? No new trades today.

questions.simple: Write it out and set it aside, because getting a worry on paper frees your head for the market.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F67) as the fallback; key is Tendler's advice, named in the question

deeper.example: Jared Tendler suggests writing for up to 15 minutes, one hour before you trade, to get some of the emotion out so you can put it away for now. Schwab notes that writing about worries before a high-pressure event frees up working memory for the task at hand.

questions.story: It's 11:30 a.m. You were sharp all morning. Now you notice you've read the same chart twice without taking it in.
questions.q: What's the call?
choices: Step away for a short break now
Push through until the close
Trade more to get your edge back
Rest after your first mistake
questions.answer: Step away for a short break now
questions.why: Take a short break, now. Reading the same chart twice without taking it in is your early warning. Don't wait until you need the break. By then you're already making mistakes. Fatigue makes it harder to control your emotions, and that's when old bad habits creep back in. Walk away, get some air, come back fresh. If the break doesn't fix it and you're just plain tired, you're done for the day. Tired means no new trades for us.
questions.lesson_line: Breaks are part of the plan. Take one before you're running on empty.

wrong.Trade more to get your edge back: More orders won't bring your focus back. They just give a tired head more chances to slip.
wrong.Push through until the close: Grinding on tired is when mistakes and old habits show up, and they cost money.
wrong.Rest after your first mistake: That's waiting until you need it. The warning sign is here now. Take the break before the mistake.

questions.simple: Take a short break now, before fatigue turns into mistakes.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F67) as the fallback

deeper.example: Jared Tendler: don't wait until you need a break. Key on early warning signs so you can take one before your energy nosedives, because fatigue decreases your ability to control your emotions. Brett Steenbarger: in the fatigued state we're more likely to make mistakes and fall into old habit patterns that cost us money.

questions.q: Saving today's trade write-ups for the weekend works just as well as doing them today.
questions.why: False. Write them up today. The minute you walk away, details start to go. Why you took it, what you saw, what you felt when it moved against you. By Saturday it's a blur and you're filling gaps from memory. We journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. The weekend review is great. It sits on top of the daily journal. It doesn't replace it.
questions.lesson_line: Write it while it's fresh. By the weekend, half of it's gone.
questions.simple: False, because details fade fast once you walk away, so write today's trades up today.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B27)
fixed before

deeper.example: Jared Tendler: as soon as you walk away, details start to disappear, and the best time to get the emotion out is soon after you're done. Brett Steenbarger reviews at the end of each trading day.

questions.story: You overslept. It's 9:25 a.m. ET, and the open is at 9:30. No warm-up, no levels, and a stock you've never studied is ripping premarket.
questions.q: What's the move?
choices: Hold off, no plan means no buy
Buy the runner before it gets away
Trade your normal size, prep later
Take a small starter position
questions.answer: Hold off, no plan means no buy
questions.why: Hold off. No plan, no buy. Every buy we make has its entry, stop and size written down before the open, and you've got none of that. You don't know where you're wrong on this stock, so you can't size it. A runner you've never studied is exactly the trade that burns you when you're rushed. Let it go. If it still looks good tonight, do the work and write the plan for tomorrow.
questions.lesson_line: No plan, no buy. Entry, stop and size go on paper before the open.

wrong.Buy the runner before it gets away: It's premarket, and we don't buy outside regular trading hours. You also have no levels, no stop and no research on it.
wrong.Trade your normal size, prep later: Prep later means trading unprepared now. A lot of trading problems start with a skipped warm-up.
wrong.Take a small starter position: Small or not, it's a buy with no stop. Without a stop you can't size it at all.

questions.simple: Hold off, because a buy with no levels, no stop and no research is a guess, not a plan.

deeper.trap: The runner is the trap. It looks like the best trade of the day because it's moving. But you know nothing about it: no levels, no stop, no research. Investor.gov: don't ever invest in anything you haven't thoroughly and independently researched. Brett Steenbarger: many trading problems occur simply because the right functions were never warmed up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, E58)
trading hours can change (NYSE 9:30 a.m. open, re-read 2026-11-12)
fixed before

questions.story: Ugly day. You moved your stop, took a big loss, and you're angry. It's 4:10 p.m. and you want to shut the laptop.
questions.q: What's your cool-down tonight?
choices: Write out what happened and why
Shut it, forget it, start fresh
Trade after hours to win it back
questions.answer: Write out what happened and why
questions.why: Write out what happened and why. On an emotional day, Tendler's goal is to keep the emotion from carrying over to tomorrow. At minimum, a brain dump: what happened, what you felt, what set it off.
questions.lesson_line: Bad days need the cool-down most. Get it on paper before you sleep.

wrong.Shut it, forget it, start fresh: Tendler: skip the cool-down and the odds of making the same mistake again go up.
wrong.Trade after hours to win it back: That's revenge trading. Investopedia's rules call it a recipe for disaster.

questions.story: Your review lists six fixes: entries, stops, size, sleep, focus and patience. You want all six fixed by tomorrow.
questions.q: Which goal do you take into tomorrow?
choices: One fix, stated specifically
Work on all six fixes at once
Just be more disciplined
No goal, just trade and see
questions.why: One fix, and make it specific. Six goals at once and none of them gets real attention. Pick the one costing you the most. Then say it so you can check it at the close, like 'every buy has its stop written down before the open.' Be more disciplined isn't a goal. It's a good intention, and you can't grade it. Work that one fix every day until it sticks. Then the next one. One thing at a time.
questions.lesson_line: One goal, specific enough to check at the close. Then the next one.

wrong.Work on all six fixes at once: Too many goals, and none of them gets proper attention. You end up fixing nothing.
wrong.Just be more disciplined: That's a good intention, not a goal. You can't check it at the close.
wrong.No goal, just trade and see: Experience alone doesn't teach much. Experience aimed at a goal, with feedback, is what moves you forward.

questions.simple: Pick one fix and say it clearly, because too many goals split your focus and vague goals rarely stick.

deeper.trap: Six fixes feels thorough, and that is the trap. Steenbarger finds that a long list of goals makes it hard to prioritise and to give each one proper attention. Pick one fix, state it so you can check it at the close, and work on it every day. The rest wait their turn.

reasons: two publishers agree (Steenbarger, Tendler); a stable idea

questions.q: A losing day after you ran your routine perfectly means the routine is broken.
questions.why: False. One red day tells you almost nothing. A routine raises your odds. It doesn't guarantee a green day. Trading's about probabilities, not certainties, so you'll lose on days you did everything right. That's normal. At the close, check one thing: whether you followed it. If you did, that's a good day, even red. Judge the routine over weeks, not one session. Change it after every loss and you'll never learn if it works.
questions.lesson_line: One red day says little about a good routine. Judge it over weeks.
questions.simple: False, because a good routine raises your odds but can't promise a win on any one day.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a process by one result. A losing day can follow a well-run routine, and a winning day can follow a sloppy one, because trading is about probabilities. Change the routine after every red day and you never learn whether it works. Ask instead: did I follow it? That is the part you control.

reasons: three publishers agree (Tendler, Schwab, Steenbarger)

questions.story: Best week of your year. You journaled every trade the same day. This weekend you plan to skip the weekly review. Things are clearly working.
questions.q: Is skipping it a problem?
choices: Yes, a good week has lessons
No, reviews are for bad weeks
No, but size up next week
Yes, the profit needs logging
questions.answer: Yes, a good week has lessons
questions.why: Yes, it's a problem. A great week is the best film you'll get. Something you did worked, and you want to know exactly what, so you can do it again on purpose. Maybe it was the setups, the patience or the entries. Find it and make it a goal to repeat. Watch the other thing too. Dropping the review when you're hot is a sign of quiet overconfidence. Next comes sizing up past the rules, and we never do that after a run of winners.
questions.lesson_line: Review the great weeks too. That's where you learn what to repeat.

wrong.No, reviews are for bad weeks: Studying your wins is how you find your best practices. The bad weeks only tell you half the story.
wrong.No, but size up next week: Skipping the review is the problem. And a hot week never earns more risk than the rules allow.
wrong.Yes, the profit needs logging: You journaled every trade the same day, so it's logged. The weekly review is for lessons, not bookkeeping.

questions.simple: Yes, because a great week shows you what to repeat, and skipping the review when you're hot is how you get sloppy.

deeper.trap: A hot streak is when the process quietly slips. Jared Tendler sees traders journal regularly, then fall off when they're doing well, a sign of subtle overconfidence. The next step can be raising risk past the rules, which we never do after a run of winners. Brett Steenbarger: studying your successes is how you define your best practices.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D45, B27)

questions.story: You slept badly and feel tired. You skipped your warm-up. Ten minutes after the open, your first trade is a loss. You want right back in.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Step away, no new trades today
Jump back in to make it back
Keep trading, tighten stops
Do the warm-up, then trade again
questions.answer: Step away, no new trades today
questions.why: Step away. You're done for the day. You were tired before that first trade, and tired means no new trades for us. The loss just proved the point. When you're tired your emotions get bigger and your ability to handle them shrinks. That itch to get it right back is revenge trading, and it turns one small loss into a bad day. Shut it down, sleep, and come back tomorrow with a real warm-up. It's one day. The market will be there.
questions.lesson_line: Tired, sick, angry or distracted: no new trades that day. A late warm-up doesn't change that.

wrong.Jump back in to make it back: That's revenge trading. Trading more to win back a loss is a recipe for disaster.
wrong.Keep trading, tighten stops: A tighter stop doesn't fix a tired head. The problem is the trader, not the stop.
wrong.Do the warm-up, then trade again: A late warm-up isn't a reset button. You're still tired, and tired means no new trades today.

questions.simple: Stop for the day, because you're tired, and a tired trader takes no new trades.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the warm-up as a reset button. Skipping it wasn't the real problem. You're tired, and tired means no new trades that day, warm-up or not. Jared Tendler: when you're tired, your emotions get bigger while your ability to deal with them is more limited.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F67): re-keyed in wave9 from Schwab's 15-minute break to F67
fixed before

questions.story: Same routine for two years. The market has gone from smooth trends to choppy swings. Your results have gone flat.
questions.q: What do you do with your routine?
choices: Rework it, keep what works
Stick with it, it worked before
Drop routines, trade on feel
Copy a top trader's routine
questions.why: Rework it, and keep what still works. A routine makes you efficient, but it can also lock you into a market that's gone. Your prep was built for smooth trends. Chop needs something different, so find the steps that keep failing and change them. Keep the ones that still pull their weight, like setting levels before the open. Running the same routine in a new market isn't more experience. It's the same year, repeated.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the routine, but review it. When the market changes, your prep changes too.

wrong.Stick with it, it worked before: It worked in the old market. Five years of experience beats one year repeated five times.
wrong.Drop routines, trade on feel: That throws out what works along with what doesn't. Routines are how you process the market efficiently.
wrong.Copy a top trader's routine: Their routine fits their strengths. Build yours on what you do best, from your own wins.

questions.simple: Rework it and keep what works, because a routine that never changes stops fitting when the market does.

deeper.example: Say your routine was built for smooth trends. In choppy swings, some steps keep failing. Keep the parts that still work and rework the rest. Brett Steenbarger: routine is the friend of efficiency and the enemy of change, and reworking old processes is what keeps traders profitable when markets go from trending to choppy.
